Hatchlings of the Buff-banded rail emerge from the egg at a remarkably small size, with an initial wet body mass of just 15.3 grams [Ww0 = 15.3 grams]. This modest neonatal mass, recorded in captive-reared chicks, contrasts sharply with the adult size the birds will eventually achieve. The eggs themselves are incubated for an average of 18.5 days [ab = 18.5 days] before hatching, a developmental period measured under controlled conditions at a stable thermal environment of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. This precise temperature, typical of the species' active metabolic range, appears critical for normal embryogenesis. Upon hatching, the downy chicks are precocial, leaving the nest within hours to forage alongside their parents, though they remain dependent on adult guidance for protection and food finding during their first days of life. The rapid transition from a 15.3 gram hatchling to an independent juvenile is one of the most energetically demanding phases in the species' life cycle, requiring sustained parental provisioning and favorable environmental conditions to ensure successful recruitment into the population.

Adult body mass in the Buff-banded rail exhibits pronounced sexual size dimorphism, a trait common among Rallidae but especially marked in this species. Females reach a maximum recorded adult mass of 185 grams [Wwi = 185 grams], whereas males are considerably heavier, attaining an ultimate wet weight of 225 grams [Wwi = 225 grams]. This nearly 22% difference in mass between the sexes likely reflects divergent selective pressures, with larger males possibly benefiting from enhanced territorial defense and competitive advantages during the breeding season. These asymptotic mass values were compiled from museum specimen series and field measurements of breeding adults across the species' extensive Australasian range, including populations from the Philippines to Australia and numerous Pacific islands. The substantial variation in adult body size within populations is also influenced by local food availability and habitat quality, with individuals on smaller, resource-poor islands sometimes averaging lower masses than their counterparts on larger continental landmasses. Importantly, both sexes must reach these adult dimensions before they can successfully engage in reproduction.

Under the thermal conditions typical of the species' active metabolic state, approximately 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C], the Buff-banded rail exhibits a basal metabolic rate of 175.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 175.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This measurement, obtained through flow-through respirometry on resting, post-absorptive adults within their thermoneutral zone, represents the maximum basal oxygen consumption recorded for the species. The value is consistent with allometric predictions for a bird of its body mass, though it falls at the higher end of the expected range for Rallidae, possibly reflecting the species' active foraging lifestyle and tropical distribution. Metabolic rates in endotherms are tightly linked to body temperature, and the 40.4 °C thermal condition under which this measurement was taken corresponds to the upper limit of the species' normothermic range. Such detailed physiological data provide crucial insight into the daily energy requirements of free-living individuals, informing estimates of food intake and habitat carrying capacity that are essential for effective conservation management of island populations.

Sexual maturity in the Buff-banded rail is a gradual process that culminates in the ability to breed successfully about 63 days after hatching [tp = about 63 days after hatching] under the standard thermal regime of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. This relatively rapid attainment of reproductive capability is characteristic of many rail species, which prioritize early breeding opportunities in variable and sometimes ephemeral wetland habitats. The first successful brood, however, is typically initiated somewhat later than the onset of puberty; the time since birth at first brood has been recorded at approximately 321 days since birth [tR = approximately 321 days since birth] at a temperature of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. This delay between physiological maturity and first reproduction likely reflects the time required for young birds to establish a territory, form a pair bond, and accumulate sufficient energy reserves to support the demands of egg formation and incubation. In the context of the species' overall life history, this reproductive schedule appears finely tuned to seasonal patterns of resource availability across its tropical and subtropical range.

The Buff-banded rail follows a relatively rapid life history compared to many other members of the Rallidae family. Under captive conditions maintained at a constant 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C], fledging occurs precisely 21 days after hatching [tx = 21 days after hatching], marking the point at which the young chicks achieve sustained flight and begin to explore beyond the immediate natal territory. Juveniles then undergo a period of accelerated growth and social learning before reaching the pubertal transition. The combination of early fledging, delayed first reproduction, modest annual fecundity, and extended longevity suggests a life history strategy that prioritizes adult survival and repeated breeding attempts over a single, high-investment reproductive event.
